A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same AutoMixer paper, including complete Appendices A–B. Text and rendered-page comparisons establish that pages 2–12 are identical; first-page differences concern authorship and the version stamp.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining experiments on eight reasoning benchmarks, checkpoint ablations, and dataset analyses in Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–6.

after.justification: v2 retains the same original experimental results and analyses, including the dataset statistics in Appendix A.

M1.justification: Sections 3–5 and Appendix B retain identical checkpoint selection, influence approximation, data regrouping, and sampling-weight procedures, including Algorithm 1.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same FineWeb/FineWeb-Edu training coverage and eight reasoning benchmarks: ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, OBQA, and WinoGrande.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains uniform, PPL, and n-gram sampling comparisons. Table 3 retains the same last-checkpoint and 10-checkpoint comparators against AutoMixer-350M.

E3.justification: Sections 4 and 6 retain identical training budgets, zero-shot evaluation, 75M/350M proxy configurations, and 350M/1.5B/3B target model configurations. No experimental protocol is added or revised.

E4.justification: The checkpoint-selection ablation, training trajectory, proxy-size analyses, and Appendix A dataset analysis are unchanged in Table 3, Figures 4–6, and Table 4.

E5.justification: Both specify two training runs with distinct random initializations and retain the same ± reporting in Tables 2–3. No run-count or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: All reported values and plotted findings are unchanged. For example, Table 2 retains AutoMixer-350M's reported average improvements of 1.93, 1.22, and 1.05 percentage points for the 350M, 1.5B, and 3B target models, respectively.

T1.justification: The empirical-risk formulation, influence derivation and approximation, checkpoint blending factors, and group influence-density definitions in Sections 4–5 are identical.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about checkpoint artifacts as data mixers, proxy-model reuse, and performance improvements of up to 1.93%.

C2.justification: The interpretations of checkpoint selection and proxy model size are identical. The limitations concerning computational overhead, dataset bias, reasoning-task coverage, and transfer across architectures and training scales are also unchanged.

D1.justification: The architecture, hardware, simulation timing and cost disclosures, data processing instructions, and Appendix B pseudocode are unchanged. No implementation or resource-access information is added.

R1.justification: The background discussion, cited works, reference list, and positioning relative to prior data-mixing and influence-estimation research are identical.

P1.justification: v2 adds Vish Vogeti to the author list and updates the arXiv version/date stamp. The scientific prose, terminology, section structure, and appendices remain identical.

P2.justification: The added author widens and recenters the first-page author line. All six figures, four tables, Algorithm 1, and the remaining page layout are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 changes authorship/version information and the author-line layout while retaining identical scientific content, evidence, explanations, and appendices. These limited front-matter edits establish no meaningful net change in the paper's overall quality.
